title: The scale
hookLine: deeds weighed, and good character the heaviest (Tirmidhi)

cards: Some companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him, once laughed at Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. He had climbed a tree, the wind caught his clothes, and his legs showed, thin as sticks.

A report in the Musnad of Ahmad says the Prophet asked what they were laughing at, and they said: his thin shins. And he answered that those legs would be heavier on the scale than the mountain of Uhud. Same legs.

teach.b: The word is mizan, a balance, a pair of scales. The Qur'an speaks of a just balance set up on the Day of Resurrection, so that no soul is wronged, and says even the weight of a mustard seed will be brought.
Surah al-Qari'ah puts it in two lines: the one whose scales are heavy will have a pleasing life; the one whose scales are light, an abyss. So what is heavy?

Jami' at-Tirmidhi records the Prophet saying, in paraphrase, that nothing is heavier on the believer's scale on the Day of Resurrection than good character, and that Allah dislikes the one who is foul and coarse in speech.
Not the longest night prayer. Not the largest gift. Good character.
Another hadith in the same collection says that by good character a person reaches the rank of one who fasts and prays.
Arabic has a word for it, husn al-khuluq, beauty of character: patience in traffic, gentleness with a slow parent, honesty when nobody would know.

teach.h: LIGHT ON THE TONGUE, HEAVY ON THE SCALE.
teach.b: And Sahih al-Bukhari closes with a hadith about two phrases, light on the tongue, heavy on the scale, beloved to the Most Merciful: subhan Allah wa bihamdihi, subhan Allah al-'azim.
Glory be to Allah and His is the praise; glory be to Allah, the Mighty. Put together, the scale works the opposite way from the world. The world weighs size, money, looks, the legs in the tree.
The mizan, in these texts, weighs a soft answer and a remembered God.

how: Muslims believe deeds will be weighed on the mizan on the Day of Resurrection, and teachers cite the hadith that nothing is heavier on it than good character; the two phrases 'light on the tongue, heavy on the scale' are part of daily remembrance.

o: the angel who writes down every deed a person does
the measure of a fair price in the marketplace
the balance on which deeds are weighed on the Day

p: a balance, a pair of scales
light on the tongue, heavy on the scale

s: in a hadith in Tirmidhi, nothing is heavier on the scale than good character
not the longest prayer or the largest gift: good character.
the Qur'an says small deeds are too light to be weighed
even the weight of a mustard seed will be brought.
the Prophet joined in laughing at Ibn Mas'ud's thin legs
he said those legs were heavier on the scale than Uhud.

games.q: you want the heaviest thing possible on your scale. by the hadith in Tirmidhi, what do you bring?
o: the longest night prayer you can manage.
the largest gift you can afford.
games.why: nothing is heavier on the believer's scale than good character; by it, another hadith says, a person reaches the rank of one who fasts and prays.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose good nature made a hard moment lighter, and stay with them for a few breaths.
Then see the moment ahead where you're most likely to be short with someone, a long line, a child at bedtime, and see yourself meeting it gently, with a slower answer and one kind sentence.
If you pray, say the two light phrases, subhan Allah wa bihamdihi, subhan Allah al-'azim; if not, rest on the word gentle.

wordCard.voice: Mizan. The balance on which deeds are weighed on the Day; in a hadith in Tirmidhi, nothing on it is heavier than good character. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a balance, a pair of scales.

carryVoice: Your line: character is heavy. Thin legs, and a heavy scale on the Day. See you tomorrow.
